Objects placed on or wedged between the strings include bolts, screws, mutes, erasers, paper, cardboard, copper strips, copper rods, aluminium bowls, rubber blocks, plastic boxes, glass rods, spoons, forks, clothes pegs, rosined fishing line, bells, chains, clip-on lamps, and drawing pins pushed into the hammer felt. The Acoustisizer takes a small grand piano and adds loudspeakers, magnetic pickups, piezoelectric contact microphones and a powered oscillator made of vibration-sensitive material. The rest of the wood and metal content of the case is not stated.
準備鋼琴可見於舞蹈音樂、打擊樂替代與多種演出與錄音場合。約翰·凱吉為舞蹈《巴卡納: The prepared piano appears in dance music, as a substitute for percussion and in many performance and recording contexts. John Cage used the technique for the dance Bacchanale because the venue had no room for a percussion ensemble, so that a single grand piano carried all the sounds; his Sonatas and Interludes are also distinguished by a different timbre on every key. Ferrante & Teicher added partly prepared piano to some tracks of an album for extra percussive effect. John Cale prepared the piano with a chain of paper clips on Tomorrow's Party, and Dave Brubeck prepared it with copper strips on Blues Roots. It also appears on solo albums, in film scores, in wind symphonies and on tour.

The prepared piano is a chordophone whose timbre is temporarily changed by placing bolts, screws, mutes, erasers and the like on or between the strings of a piano. The player does not only press keys but also works on the strings directly; John Cage used the technique in the dance music Bacchanale because the Seattle venue could not fit a percussion ensemble, so that a single pianist came close to a percussion band; in Sonatas and Interludes each key has its own timbre, the original pitch is not always recognisable, and the soft pedal (una corda) adds further variation. Ferrante & Teicher and others also used it on albums.
準備鋼琴的發明通常追溯至 John Cage，1940年為舞蹈《Bacchana: The invention of the prepared piano is usually traced to John Cage, who used it in 1940 for the dance Bacchanale because the venue could not fit a percussion ensemble. Forerunners include Henry Cowell's string piano and the use of paper to damp the strings by Delage, Villa-Lobos and Ravel. Between 1950 and 1980 a number of musicians used it on recordings; from the 1980s Cor Fuhler, Roger Miller, Aphex Twin and Hauschka and others kept extending it. Important developments include the nailed piano, which cannot be fully restored, and Bob Fenger's Acoustisizer of 1983, which combines amplification and pickups.
準備鋼琴的音色具有獨特的非傳統性質，呈現出金屬質感與打擊樂的特性。根據放置物體的: The prepared piano has a distinctly unconventional timbre, with a metallic quality and a percussive character. Depending on the material and position of the objects, the timbre ranges from a bright, harsh metallic clang to a dull, soft drum-like boom, combining the warm depth of the piano with the crispness of the xylophone. Its range covers the whole of the piano, but each note changes timbre in its own way because of the interference of the preparation. Its resonance differs from the sustaining-pedal effect of a traditional piano: the complex vibration of the soundboard produces richly layered overtones. Compared with the singing quality of an ordinary piano, the prepared piano is closer to the texture of a percussion ensemble; compared with the harp it has more of the cold hardness of metal and machinery, creating a distinctive sound world between the keyboard and percussion.
